qc.label_under_test: Plural pronoun for a romantic couple right after the partner is introduced by a conjunction (his wife, Lucy, and | their; met him and | they started dating); a group of coworkers or companies in the same frame stays quiet

neighbours.label: a plural pronoun for a pair that a sentence has just formed, whatever the relationship ('with his wife, Emily, and their', 'called his father, and they', 'sat beside me and we'), as against a plural pronoun for a group that was plural from the start
fire: Dana lives in Reno with her sister, Kate, and their old cat.
Tom called his father last night, and they talked for an hour.
A stranger sat beside me on the train and we talked all the way.
Paul moved to Austin with his wife, Ana, and their baby.
My boss hired Lee in June, and they argued from the first day.
She married Omar in spring, and they settled near the coast.
Ruth took her nephew to the fair, where they rode the wheel.
He met Nina at a party, and they danced until midnight.
quiet: The sailors reached the harbor, where they rested for a week.
All the farmers sold wheat, and they bought new tools.
Several nurses left early because they had a long drive.
Most tourists like this beach since they can swim safely.
Those engineers built bridges, and their work still stands.
Young monkeys play in trees, where they learn to climb.
The players lost again, and their coach looked tired.
Many birds fly south when they sense the cold.

short: plural pronoun for a pair just formed
notes: QC from a seeded sample, proposing a broader label. The current label says a romantic couple. Probe: spouse 0.989 and 0.805, but brother 0.887, son 0.929 and strangers on a flight (' we') 0.734, so the romance looks unnecessary; 'The boys ran ... they' 0.052. Fire items are pairs that are not couples, plus couples; near misses are plural pronouns for a group that was already plural, with no pair just formed. Card's top examples include non-romantic pairs too.
